hints: Remember what a Boltzmann distribution is showing, the spread of energies among a fixed number of molecules.
The x-axis is molecular energy, so the y-axis must count how many molecules have each energy.
Higher temperature shifts the peak to the right and flattens it, as more molecules gain higher energy, so look for the lower, broader peak shifted right.
walkthrough:
**Recall the axes of the Boltzmann distribution**

Think of it as a census of energies. We put energy along the x-axis and count molecules up the y-axis.

$$x = \text{molecular energy (or speed)}, \quad y = \text{number of molecules with that energy}$$

**Apply the effect of higher temperature**

Heating gives molecules more kinetic energy on average. So the most probable energy (the peak) moves to the right.

Because the total number of molecules is the same, the area under each curve is the same, so the hotter curve must be lower and broader.

**Compare T1 and T2 on the diagram**

$T_1$ is tall, narrow and peaks at lower $x$. $T_2$ is shorter, broader and peaks at higher $x$, with a longer tail to high energy.

That shape is the classic signature of the higher temperature, so y is number of molecules and $T_2$ is hotter.

options.A: The y-axis is correct as number of molecules, but $T_1$ is not the higher temperature. $T_1$ has the taller, narrower peak at lower energy, which is the colder sample.
options.B: Correct on both parts. The y-axis counts number (or fraction) of molecules with a given energy, and $T_2$ is hotter because its peak is lower, broader and shifted to higher energy.
options.C: Both parts are wrong. Molecular energy goes on the x-axis, not the y-axis, and $T_1$ is the lower temperature curve with the high narrow peak.
options.D: $T_2$ is indeed the higher temperature, but the y-axis is not molecular energy. Energy is plotted on the x-axis, while the y-axis shows how many molecules possess each energy.
